commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods depend on conditions established elsewhere: the parse
helpers slice input on the assumption that the command word is already
matched, the task list converts a 1-based number after checkNumber has
vetted it, and DateRange reads its two ends in order. Nothing states
those assumptions, so breaking one produces a wrong answer rather than
a failure -- a reversed date range simply matches no tasks.

Add assertions recording eight such assumptions, each at the point it
must hold. Assertions suit these because they describe what is true
when the code is correct. User mistakes stay with FF15Exception, which
is reported and recoverable. Two of the eight cover the empty-varargs
call that showMessage and add now silently accept.

Assertions are disabled unless asked for, so pass -ea to the run task.
Gradle already enables them when running the tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the dead standardInput setting from the build
commitResults.messageBody:
The run task pipes System.in into the application, from when gradlew
run started the console session. The entry point is now the JavaFX
launcher, which never reads standard input, so the setting changes
nothing about what the build produces.

Delete it. Configuration that does nothing still costs a reader the
effort of working out what it is for, and the console main can still
be run directly with java -cp when it is wanted.

commitResults.messageTitle: Punctuate every @throws description
commitResults.messageBody:
Javadoc @param descriptions all end with a full stop, but the @throws
descriptions sitting beside them in the same comment do not. A single
block therefore mixes both styles, which reads as an oversight rather
than a decision.

The coding standard names only parameter descriptions, so neither form
breaks it. Consistency inside one comment is worth more than the
narrow reading, and both @return tags were already punctuated by hand,
which suggests the wider rule was always the intent.

Punctuate the 16 remaining @throws descriptions. Parser's spans two
lines, so its full stop goes at the end of the continuation rather
than after the first line.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the argument markers used when parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
parseDeadline and parseEvent each write their marker twice: once to
find it with indexOf, and again to skip past it with length(). Six
literals stand in for three markers, and changing one without its
partner slices the description at the wrong offset -- a wrong answer
rather than an error.

Pull the three markers out as constants, so each is written once and
the substring arithmetic reads against a name. The literals were also
the only record of the /by, /from and /to syntax, which is worth
stating plainly for anyone adding a command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Simplify the guard on a malformed event command
commitResults.messageBody:
The guard in parseEvent tests three conditions in one expression, and
the last of them, toIndex < fromIndex, requires the reader to work out
that it means the user typed /to before /from.

Name each condition. The guard then reads as the three ways an event
command can be malformed, which is what the message it throws already
says in words.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the field counts of the save format
commitResults.messageBody:
parseTask calls requireFieldCount with a bare 3, 4 or 5, each followed
by a comment saying which fields the number covers. The numbers carry
no meaning on their own, and the comments have to be kept in step with
the format by hand.

Replace them with named constants and drop the comments they made
redundant. The name now says what the number counts, at the one place
the save format is defined.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Task's fields private
commitResults.messageBody:
Task exposes description and isDone as protected, so any subclass may
read or write them directly. No subclass does: Todo, Deadline and
Event pass the description to the constructor and reach the rest
through toString and toFileFormat.

Narrow both to private, and make description final since nothing
reassigns it. Widening access later is easy; discovering which of
three subclasses quietly writes to a field is not.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams where a loop only filters or maps
commitResults.messageBody:
Four loops exist only to filter or transform a collection: the two
searches in TaskList, the save-format conversion in Storage, and the
command-word lookup in CommandWord. Each spends most of its lines on
the mechanics of accumulating a result rather than on the condition
that decides what goes in it.

Rewrite them as streams, so each reads as the one operation it
performs. CommandWord.match gains a small matches() helper: the
condition it tests needs four lines of explanation, which belongs in a
named method rather than inside a lambda.

The two TaskList searches collect into an ArrayList rather than using
toList(), because callers are handed a copy they may modify, and two
tests rely on that by clearing the result. Storage.load is left as a
loop: parseTask throws a checked exception, which map() cannot carry.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a contact model and list
commitResults.messageBody:
A contact is not a task: it has no done state, no dates, and nothing to
mark. Extending Task would give every contact behaviour that makes no
sense for it, and would put contacts in the middle of the task list.

Add a separate package holding a Contact and the list that owns them.
The list mirrors TaskList deliberately -- the same 1-based numbering,
the same guard against numbers nobody has, the same assertions -- so
anyone who knows one knows the other.

Only the name is required. A phone or an email left out is stored empty
and never shown back to the user, so a contact with just a name shows as
just that name rather than as a row of blanks.

commitResults.messageTitle: Carry a contact list through the program
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing outside the new package can reach a contact: Storage owns one
file and one format, Command.execute takes only a TaskList, and the Ui
knows how to show tasks alone.

Give Storage a second path, widen execute by one parameter, and build
the contact list beside the task list at startup. Each command uses
whichever list it works on and ignores the other, which keeps one
execute for all of them rather than a second hierarchy dispatched on by
type. These three changes are one change in practice, since none of them
compiles without the others.

Contacts live in their own file so the task format is untouched and a
save file written before contacts existed still loads. A saved contact
always writes all three fields, so a name-only one ends in two empty
fields -- which is why the split passes -1 as its limit, the default
having dropped them and lost the name. The two files are read in
separate try blocks, so a damaged one does not cost the user the other.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the contact commands and their parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
The contact list is reachable from a command but nothing builds one, so
there is still no way for the user to record anyone.

Add add, list, delete and find behind a single 'contact' word rather
than four top-level verbs, so the feature groups under one word and adds
no more as it grows. Task find is left alone: it searches descriptions
only, and contact find searches names only, so neither surprises the
user with the other's results.

The /phone and /email markers may come in either order and either may be
left out. Both are checked lightly -- a phone's characters, and an email
having one @ with text on both sides -- which catches an obvious mistake
without refusing an unusual but legitimate value. Markers carry a
leading space so a name may contain one, and the line is padded before
searching so that "contact add /phone 123" is a missing name rather than
a contact named after the marker.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover contacts in the UI test plan
commitResults.messageBody:
The plan drove every command the chatbot had, so the console runner
exercised the whole command set. Contacts were not in it.

Add cases for each sub-command, for the input each one rejects, and for
two things worth pinning down: find does not match a contact, and list
does not show one. The plan still ends with everything deleted, so both
save files are left empty for the next run.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #4 from My2h/branch-D-Contacts
commitResults.messageBody: D-Contacts

commitResults.messageTitle: Show the two sides of the chat asymmetrically
commitResults.messageBody:
Both sides of the conversation are drawn the same way: a bubble beside a
face, mirrored. That is the layout for two people talking. This is one
person talking to a program, and showing the user their own face beside
every line adds nothing they need and eats a third of the width.

Drop the user's picture altogether and give the two sides different
treatments: the user's lines are solid accent bubbles on the right, and
FF15's replies are quiet frosted panels on the left beside its face, the
way a messaging app shows the other party. DialogBox now builds each
kind explicitly rather than building one and flipping it, so the two
sides can diverge further without the flip having to undo anything.

The user picture is removed from the resources, since nothing shows it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show FF15's face as a small circle at the bubble's tail
commitResults.messageBody:
FF15's picture is a 72px square beside every reply. At that size it is a
portrait, and in a window 400px wide it takes a fifth of each line away
from the words. The picture is 860 by 946, so it is also not square, and
squares of it show flat edges where the frame does not fit.

Crop the picture to its central square, shrink it to 36px, and clip it
to a circle. It now reads as a marker of who is speaking rather than a
portrait, which is all it needs to do when the speakers never change.
It also sits at the bottom of the bubble, where the tail points, so a
long reply reads as coming from the face rather than floating above it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Draw an error reply so it cannot be skimmed past
commitResults.messageBody:
An error looks exactly like every other reply: the same panel in the same
colour, in the same place. The only thing marking it out is the word
"AYY!!!" at the start, which is easy to miss once the conversation is
long and the eye is scanning for the newest bubble.

Have FF15 remember whether its last reply was an error, and have the
window draw such a reply in warning colours with a firmer edge. The
words are unchanged, so the console session and the test plan are
unaffected; only the presentation differs. FF15 already knows which
replies are errors, since they are the ones that came through a catch
block, so the window needs no guessing from the text.

commitResults.messageTitle: Tighten the spacing and refresh the palette
commitResults.messageBody:
The window is 400px wide and most replies are lists, so every pixel
given to padding, gaps and the composer is a pixel taken from the words.
The violet theme also puts white text on a bright gradient for the
user's own lines, which is the lowest-contrast pairing in the window.

Cut the gaps between bubbles, the insets around the log, and the height
of the composer, and shrink the bubble padding, so the same window shows
noticeably more of the conversation. Move to a near-black slate with a
lime-to-mint accent, with dark text on the bright bubbles and light text
on the muted ones, so both sides read at a glance. Set a modern system
font stack and a touch of line spacing, since the replies that matter
most are several lines of task listings.

The scroll bar drops to a hairline, and disabled controls dim so the
farewell pause after 'bye' is visibly the window winding down.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the window resize and the bubbles follow
commitResults.messageBody:
The window can be dragged larger but nothing inside it moves: the root
pane pins its maximum size to its preferred size, and every dialog box
is a fixed 400px wide, so a bigger window is the same small chat with
empty space around it.

Unpin the root so it fills whatever size the window is given, and drop
the fixed width from the dialog boxes so each row spans the log. A
bubble's width is then bound to a share of its row, so a long message
wraps at four-fifths of the window rather than running edge to edge --
wide enough to use the space, short enough to still look like a bubble
on one side. On FF15's side the face and the gap after it come off the
row first, so its bubbles and the user's wrap at the same point.

The minimum size keeps the composer and a few lines of chat usable; the
old minimum height of 220 left room for the composer and little else.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give the composer a voice and some manners
commitResults.messageBody:
The window is functional and a little blank. The composer says "Message
FF15...", the button says "Send", the title says "FF15", and the cursor
starts nowhere in particular, so the first thing a user does is click
into the text field.

Put the cursor in the composer at launch, light the send button up only
when there is something to send, let Escape clear a half-typed line,
and drop a blank line rather than sending it. Then let the empty
composer talk: the hint changes after every message, cycling through
office small talk in the spirit of the face in the corner, and once the
user says bye the composer clocks out with a reminder about timesheets.
The window title now introduces FF15 by its proper job title.

The hints are plain text on purpose. JavaFX 17 draws emoji unreliably,
and a hint that renders as empty boxes is worse than no hint at all.

commitResults.messageTitle: Loosen up the greeting
commitResults.messageBody:
The console greeting opens with "Eh hello bro", which reads as a
placeholder next to the voice the window now has.

Open with "Whazzup" instead, and update the test plan's startup case,
which is the one place the exact wording is checked.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #6 from My2h/branch-A-BetterGui
commitResults.messageBody: A-BetterGui

commitResults.messageTitle: Introduce FF15 as Michael's assistant
commitResults.messageBody:
FF15 greets the user with "Whazzup" and signs off with "Okie bye bye",
which is a voice but not a character. The face beside every reply has
been Michael Scott's since the GUI arrived, and the window's hints have
been his for a while; the chatbot itself has not caught up.

Have FF15 introduce itself as the Assistant to the Regional Manager --
correcting itself from "Assistant Regional Manager" the way the show
does -- and make clear that the Regional Manager is the user. From here
on FF15 talks in Michael's voice, and the user is the boss it answers
to, which is also how it signs off. The window title says the same. The
name FF15 stays: it is the product, and this is who it is when it talks.

commitResults.messageTitle: Have Michael react to tasks the way Michael would
commitResults.messageBody:
Every task command is acknowledged the same way: "Got it. I've added
this task", "Noted. I've removed this task", "Here are the tasks in
your list". It is polite and it is nobody in particular.

Give each reply Michael's reaction. A todo gets "That's what she said",
every time, because he cannot help it. An event gets "Am I invited?",
because he needs to be. A deadline gets a flat "Got it", because he
does not rate them. Marking is a Dundie, unmarking is Jan, deleting is
Toby, an empty list is also Toby, and finding things makes him Michael
Scarn. The list header now addresses the office.

The reply to adding a task therefore depends on what was added, which
the Ui decides by looking at the task; that is presentation choosing a
phrase, so it lives in the Ui rather than the model. The task counts
are unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Have Michael handle contacts and mistakes his way
commitResults.messageBody:
Errors open with "AYY!!!" and close with "bro", and the contact replies
are the task replies with the noun swapped. None of it is Michael.

Open every error with "No. GOD. NO." -- the one line of his everyone
knows, and short enough to lead a message that the window already
paints red. Rewrite the messages themselves so the excuse is his: he
knows numbers because he runs a branch, he knows dates because he has
been on many, he knows phones because he has a Blackberry. A saved file
that will not load is an IT problem, and he cannot remember the IT
guy's name. Contacts are friends, and losing one is being dead to him.

The examples that show the user the right syntax are all kept; the
character is in the words around them, not in place of them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Dress the window as a paper company
commitResults.messageBody:
The window is lime and mint, which says startup. Michael runs a
regional branch of a paper company, and the window should say so
before he does.

Swap the accent to Dunder Mifflin blue for the user's bubbles and the
send button, and give Michael's replies a paper-cream tint in place of
plain grey, so the two sides read as you and the paper company. The
window and taskbar now carry his face as the icon, and the button says
"Send." with a full stop, because that is how he says things.

The composer's hints now alternate between a Michael line and a real
example of what to type, so a new user is never more than one hint away
from a command that works. The font stays: he is not a font guy.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #7 from My2h/branch-A-Personality
commitResults.messageBody: A-Personality

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject an impossible date even when a time follows it
commitResults.messageBody:
A deadline for 2019-02-30 is rejected, but a deadline for
2019-02-30 1800 is accepted and quietly stored as Feb 28. The
date-only path parses with ISO_LOCAL_DATE, which is strict; the
date-and-time path parses with a pattern, whose default "smart"
resolution rolls an impossible day back to the last real one without
a word. The user asked for the 30th and got the 28th.

Resolve the pattern strictly too, so both paths reject the same input.
Strict resolution needs the proleptic year field, so the pattern says
uuuu rather than yyyy; the saved format is unchanged for any real date.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the readable lines when a save file has a bad one
commitResults.messageBody:
A save file with one line that cannot be parsed fails to load, the
session starts with an empty list, and the next save writes that empty
list over the file. One damaged line -- from a hand edit, or a crash
mid-write -- silently destroys every task that was fine. A test even
enshrined this as "throws rather than keeping half the file".

Load line by line, keeping every line that parses and noting each that
does not, with its number and the reason. The load returns both, and
startup reports the skipped lines before carrying on with the rest.
The bad line is dropped at the next save, which the user has been told
about, and nothing they could still have is lost.

Both loads now share one reader that takes a line parser, so the task
and contact files get the same treatment from the same code. A file
that cannot be read at all is still an IOException and still starts
that list empty; this change is only about files that can be read but
not entirely understood.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse the save file's separator in anything the user types
commitResults.messageBody:
The save file separates fields with " | ". A description containing it
saves without complaint and splits into extra fields on the way back,
so "read | book" reloads as "read" and the rest is gone. StorageTest
has recorded this since the file format was written.

Refuse "|" in descriptions, contact names and contact emails at input,
with a message that says why. It is one character and one rule, and a
user meets it at most once. Escaping it in the file would let anything
through, but at the cost of escape and unescape logic in Storage and a
set of tests for it, which is more machinery than one character earns.

The StorageTest that documents the limit is kept, reworded to say the
parser now guards it, so the limit stays stated rather than assumed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Forgive the shape of a command line, reject its substance
commitResults.messageBody:
The parser is strict about things a user cannot easily see: "list "
with a trailing space is an unknown command, and so is " list". Runs of
spaces inside a description are stored as typed, so "read  book" is
saved and listed with the gap. An empty line is reported as a command
nobody understands. And a marker given twice -- "/by 2019-12-02 /by
2019-12-03" -- is not noticed as such: the first is taken as the split
and the message then blames the date for not being one.

Trim the line and collapse runs of spaces before anything looks at it,
so a stray space never costs the user a command and a description is
stored the way it reads. Say so when the line was empty. And check
each marker appears at most once before using it, so the message names
the real mistake.

The test plan's leading-space case documented the old strictness as a
feature; it now expects the command to work.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse a task the list already has, and an event with no duration
commitResults.messageBody:
Typing the same task twice adds it twice. It is almost always a slip --
a double press of Enter, a forgotten earlier add -- and the list then
carries two identical lines the user has to notice and prune. An event
that ends the moment it starts is accepted as well, and even has a
test saying so; an event with no duration is not an event.

Give tasks a notion of being the same: the same kind, the same
description, and the same dates, ignoring whether either is done,
since the question is "do I have this?" rather than "have I done it?".
Adding a task the list already holds is refused with the number of
the one it duplicates. Contacts are left alone on purpose: two people
can share a name, and the user chose to allow that.

Reject an event whose end is the same moment as its start, alongside
the existing check for one that ends before it starts. A date-only
value is the start of its day, so "/to 2019-12-05" is the same moment
as "/from 2019-12-05 0000" and is caught too.

TaskTime gains equals and hashCode, since two tasks are the same only
if their times are, and "the same" for a time means the same instant
typed the same way -- a date-only value and that day at 0000 print
differently and so count as different.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what is wrong with a file that cannot be read or written
commitResults.messageBody:
When "data" exists as a file rather than a folder, saving fails with
the message "data". When data/ff15.txt is a folder, loading fails with
"data\ff15.txt". Both are the bare path from the exception, and neither
tells the user what about that path is the problem.

Check for the two shapes of trouble a user is likely to cause by hand
-- a file where the folder should be, and a folder where the file
should be -- and say which it is. A file the user is not allowed to
read or write is reported as a permissions problem rather than a
path. The exceptions are wrapped, not swallowed, so the cause is still
there for anyone debugging.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #8 from My2h/branch-A-MoreErrorHandling
commitResults.messageBody: A-MoreErrorHandling

commitResults.messageTitle: Measure test coverage with JaCoCo
commitResults.messageBody:
"Cover nearly all code that can be tested" needs a number, and there
is no way to get one. Which classes the suite reaches, and which lines
in them, is a guess.

Add the JaCoCo plugin and wire its report to run after the tests. The
GUI package is excluded from the figures: it is tested by hand, and
counting it would only lower a number it cannot move. Run
"gradlew jacocoTestReport" and open build/reports/jacoco/test/html.

First measurement, before any new tests: 82% of lines and 84% of
branches. FF15 is at zero, Ui at half, and four commands are reached
only on one of their two paths.

commitResults.messageTitle: Report a deadline or event with no description as such
commitResults.messageBody:
The coverage report shows the "needs a description" branches for
deadline and event can never run. The line is trimmed before the
marker is looked for, and the marker carries a leading space, so a
line that opens with the marker -- "deadline /by 2019-12-02" -- never
matches it and is reported as having no /by. The test plan documents
this as a known edge. It is the same fault that once made "contact add
/phone 123" a contact named after its marker, fixed there and not here.

Pad the line with a space before searching, as the contact parser
already does. The marker is then found where it opens the line, the
description is seen to be empty, and the user is told the thing that is
actually missing. The plan case now expects the message that was always
meant for it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test FF15 as its two front ends use it
commitResults.messageBody:
FF15 is the one class both the window and the console talk to, and
the only class with no tests at all. The greeting, the reply per line,
the two flags the window reads after each reply, and the console loop
itself are exercised only by running the program.

Test it the way each front end uses it. For the window: the greeting,
including the three things it can carry -- a skipped line, an
unreadable task file, an unreadable contact file; a reply for a good
command, a bad one, and one whose save fails, each with the error flag
where it should be; bye setting the finished flag; and a task
surviving into a new instance. For the console: standard input fed a
short session, and the whole printed transcript checked, including
that an error or a failed save part way through does not end it.

Each test gets its own folder and a silenced console, so none can
touch the real save files or clutter the test output.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test every message the Ui can show
commitResults.messageBody:
Half of Ui is untested: the loading errors, the skipped-line report in
its singular and plural forms, the farewell, the contact replies, the
block framing, and reading a line from the console. Most of these are
seen only when something has gone wrong, which is exactly when nobody
has watched them run.

Test each method for both things it produces: the console output,
captured from standard output and checked for its indentation and
divider lines, and the transcript the window reads, checked for the
words alone. The two must carry the same words and different framing,
and that is now asserted rather than assumed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the remaining commands and branches
commitResults.messageBody:
Four commands are reached on only one of their two paths: list and
contact list only with something in the list, on only with a match,
and exit never through execute. A few branches elsewhere are likewise
never taken: equals against itself or against something that is not a
TaskTime, isSameAs failing on the description before it reaches the
dates, and the varargs guards on add.

Give each command its own test class exercising both paths through a
real Ui and reading the transcript back, and add the missing branch
cases to the existing classes. The guard tests are worth having: they
are what proves add() with nothing does not pass silently.

With this the suite stands at 304 tests, covering 99% of lines and
95% of branches outside the GUI, up from 82% and 84%. What remains is
the no-argument constructor and main, which use the real save files;
the assertion failure branches, which cannot be reached without
breaking a precondition; and the permission-denied catches, which
cannot be provoked reliably on Windows.

commitResults.messageBody: A-MoreTesting

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the command typed in the missing-number example
commitResults.messageBody:
"delete" with no number replies "e.g. mark 2". The example is
hardcoded to mark, so for delete and unmark it demonstrates a
different command from the one the user was in the middle of.

Build the example from the command word that was typed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Lift the duration rules out of parseEvent
commitResults.messageBody:
parseEvent runs to 33 lines and works at several levels at once: it
slices the line around the markers, checks the text, parses the two
times, and then rules on whether they make an event. The last of those
is two checks with their own messages, and it is the part most likely
to grow.

Move the duration rules into requireSomeDuration. parseEvent now reads
as the sequence of steps it is, each at one level, and sits under the
thirty-line guideline again.

commitResults.messageTitle: Wrap the lines over the soft length limit
commitResults.messageBody:
Fourteen lines sit between the standard's soft limit of 110 characters
and its hard limit of 120. Checkstyle enforces only the hard limit, so
they pass, but the soft limit is the one the standard asks for.

Wrap them. No text changes; a few long messages become two string
literals joined with +, which is how the rest of the file already does
it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Compare an event's kind before casting the other task
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding any task to a list that holds an event crashes with a
ClassCastException. Event.isSameAs casts the other task to Event
before asking the superclass whether the two are even the same kind,
so the cast fails on a Todo or a Deadline. Deadline.isSameAs asks
first and casts second, which is why only the event side breaks.

Ask first, as Deadline does. Every list that holds an event was
affected, so the JUnit tests and the UI plan each gain a case that
adds a task of another kind after an event.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the jar grant itself native access
commitResults.messageBody:
Running java -jar ff15.jar on Java 25 prints four warnings before
the window opens, because JavaFX loads its native libraries through
a method the JDK now restricts. The Enable-Native-Access manifest
attribute is how a jar declares that permission up front.

Declare it in the shadow jar, so the app starts with a clean
terminal, which is also what a grader sees first.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what FF15 is in the user guide's intro
commitResults.messageBody:
The intro described FF15 as a regional manager who thinks he is
your assistant. It is the other way round: the user is the Regional
Manager and FF15 is the Assistant to the Regional Manager, with
Michael Scott's sense of humour.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the boolean after the question it answers
commitResults.messageBody:
acceptsArguments does not read as a yes-or-no. canTakeArguments
does, which is what the standard asks of a boolean's name.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split ParserTest by what each test is about
commitResults.messageBody:
ParserTest had grown to 649 lines covering four things: which
command a line becomes, what it was given, which lines are refused,
and the contact commands. A class that long is hard to find a test
in, and the automated code-quality report flagged it.

Move the shared harness into ParserTestBase, and divide the tests
into ParserTest (lines that parse), ParserRejectionTest (lines that
are refused) and ContactParserTest (the contact commands). No test
changed; all 307 still run.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse a contact the list already has
commitResults.messageBody:
An add of a task refuses an exact repeat and names the one it
repeats, but an add of a contact took anything, so the two halves of
the product disagreed. Refuse a contact identical in every field,
the same way. A name alone is not enough to be a repeat: two people
can share one, so John with a second phone number is a new contact.
